We supported school-based delivery and church-based sensitization to build comfort and confidence about the HPV vaccine among girls and those around them. post_message: In #Cameroon’s Nylon Health District, low #HPV vaccination rates posed a significant risk, especially given the high burden of cervical and other HPV-related cancers.   Routine immunization services were limited in reach, missed opportunities for vaccination were common, and low awareness and mistrust among some parents and health workers posed additional barriers.   To tackle these challenges, Nylon Health District launched a catalytic program — supported by Sabin and the World Health Organization — to improve HPV vaccination coverage by engaging schools, communities, and health facilities.   The results? 2,681 adolescents — 2.6 times the target — received the vaccine. Dive into Jeanne Liliane Mbengue’s case study on how the team achieved this milestone ⤵   https://bit.ly/3YNfw6n

post_message: “Caregivers used to wait for vaccine teams. Now they remind each other and bring their children early.”   Despite ongoing national and state immunization programs in #Nigeria, many children — especially in hard-to-reach and underserved communities — remain unvaccinated due to limited tracking systems, gender barriers, and weak community engagement. post_message: The Sabin Vaccine Institute announced it has completed enrollment in all six Phase 2 clinical trials for its cAd3-Marburg Vaccine and its cAd3-Sudan Ebolavirus Vaccine candidates.  There are no licensed vaccines for protection against disease caused by Marburg virus or the Sudan virus strain of Ebola. Both are highly contagious hemorrhagic fever diseases that can have a high fatality rate of up to 88%.    Phase 2 clinical trials to evaluate the safety and immunogenicity of the two monovalent vaccines, both on the cAd3 platform, began in healthy volunteers in Africa in 2023 and in the United States in 2025. The African trials, with sites in Kenya and Uganda, completed participant follow-up last year and reporting activities are progressing. The U.S. trials completed enrollment last month.  In addition, Sabin’s cAd3-Marburg Vaccine has been used in Phase 2 rapid response outbreak clinical trials in Africa — more than 1,700 participants enrolled in 2024 during an outbreak in Rwanda, and more than 500 participants enrolled beginning last December for Ethiopia’s first-ever Marburg outbreak.   Learn more ⤵️  https://ow.ly/K19e50YrNbg

post_message: The Sabin Vaccine Institute announced it has completed enrollment in all six Phase 2 clinical trials for its cAd3-Marburg Vaccine and its cAd3-Sudan Ebolavirus Vaccine candidates.  There are no licensed vaccines for protection against disease caused by Marburg virus or the Sudan virus strain of Ebola. Both are highly contagious hemorrhagic fever diseases that can have a high fatality rate of up to 88%.    Phase 2 clinical trials to evaluate the safety and immunogenicity of the two monovalent vaccines, both on the cAd3 platform, began in healthy volunteers in Africa in 2023 and in the United States in 2025. The African trials, with sites in Kenya and Uganda, completed participant follow-up last year and reporting activities are progressing. The U.S. trials completed enrollment last month.  In addition, Sabin’s cAd3-Marburg Vaccine has been used in Phase 2 rapid response outbreak clinical trials in Africa — more than 1,700 participants enrolled in 2024 during an outbreak in Rwanda, and more than 500 participants enrolled beginning last December for Ethiopia’s first-ever Marburg outbreak.   Learn more ⤵️ https://ow.ly/VYva50YrNc7

post_message: “There is no need for the vaccine because hunger will kill my child before any vaccine-preventable disease does.”  Sabin's Boost Community is made up of immunization professionals in all parts of the world. For member Fri Delphine Chifor, who works in parts of Cameroon where conflict has stripped families of safety, income, and access to basic services, vaccines remain one of the few consistent shields children still have. But getting vaccinated can often seem like a secondary concern as parents grapple with urgent questions of where they will sleep tonight or how they will find their next meal.  Chifor shares how  the Cameroon Baptist Convention Health Services Immunization Program started intentionally shifting the way they engaged with families, addressing what mattered most to them first and offering essential vaccines at the same time.   The impact was immediate — not only did they vaccinate more than 163,000 children in less than a year, but they also screened thousands for malnutrition, gave away mosquito nets and medications, and provided more than 13,000 caregivers with nutrition and vaccine education.  Read the full story at the link in our bio.

post_message: English physician Dr. Edward Jenner is credited with creating the first vaccination. In 1796, he used material from cowpox (a disease related to smallpox) to inoculate 8-year-old James Phipps. Two months later, Jenner exposed Phipps to smallpox, but the child did not get the disease.  Vaccines have now saved an estimated 154 million lives — that's the equivalent of six lives every minute for the past 50 years — and the vast majority of lives saved were infants. Today, childhood vaccinations prevent an estimated 4 million deaths annually.  Learn more about the history and impact of vaccines, and how they work at the link in our bio.

post_message: Seeing headlines about the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak? Kelly Warfield, Sabin’s President of Research & Development and an expert on this kind of virus, explains why not all Ebola vaccines are the same, and why more research in this area is so needed. ⤵️  “Vaccines developed against Ebola Zaire (EBOV) or Ebola Sudan (SUDV) may not be effective against disease caused by Ebola Bundibugyo (BDBV), such as the ongoing outbreak in DRC and Uganda, because these viruses are genetically and antigenically distinct species within the Ebolavirus genus.    Most Ebola vaccines induce targeted immune responses — particularly antibodies and T cell responses — against the viral glycoprotein (GP) of a specific species. Because the GP sequence and antigenic structure differ between Zaire, Sudan, and Bundibugyo viruses, immune responses elicited by a vaccine targeting one species may not adequately recognize or neutralize another.   While there is some early data indicating ways we might achieve protection against BDBV with existing EBOV and SUDV vaccines, further research is needed to determine whether any licensed Ebola Zaire and/or investigational Sudan vaccines can provide meaningful protection against the distinct Bundibugyo virus. Additionally, new vaccine candidates specifically targeting BDBV should be generated and tested to help address the growing threat of the virus.”  More on the Bundibugyo outbreak from the New York Times:  https://ow.ly/t1UO50Z1H39

post_message: Switching from one vaccine to another is just a matter of out with the old, in with the new, right? Not exactly.   As more than 30 co-authors, including Sabin's Kate Hopkins, PhD, MPH, report in "Accelerating Evidence-Informed Vaccine Introductions: Lessons from the Hexavalent Early Adopters Workshop" in the new issue of the journal Vaccines, there are multiple considerations when bringing a new immunization into a country's immunization schedule, including complex system changes requiring coordinated governance, reliable data systems, domestic financing, and multisectoral collaboration.  The paper presents evidence-based insights on making a successful switch from National Immunization Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs) and Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI) programs of 10 African countries, as well as World Health Organization African Region, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, and consortium partners, who gathered in Senegal last November. It shows the power of Sabin's Regional Peer Learning model/capabilities and helps strengthen policy and operational readiness for countries at different stages of decision-making, planning, and implementation. post_message: Seeing headlines about the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak? Kelly Warfield, Sabin’s President of Research & Development and an expert on this kind of virus, explains why not all Ebola vaccines are the same, and why more research in this area is so needed. ⤵️  “Vaccines developed against Ebola Zaire (EBOV) or Ebola Sudan (SUDV) may not be effective against disease caused by Ebola Bundibugyo (BDBV), such as the ongoing outbreak in DRC and Uganda, because these viruses are genetically and antigenically distinct species within the Ebolavirus genus.   Most Ebola vaccines induce targeted immune responses — particularly antibodies and T cell responses — against the viral glycoprotein (GP) of a specific species. Because the GP sequence and antigenic structure differ between Zaire, Sudan, and Bundibugyo viruses, immune responses elicited by a vaccine targeting one species may not adequately recognize or neutralize another.   While there is some early data indicating ways we might achieve protection against BDBV with existing EBOV and SUDV vaccines, further research is needed to determine whether any licensed Ebola Zaire and/or investigational Sudan vaccines can provide meaningful protection against the distinct Bundibugyo virus. Additionally, new vaccine candidates specifically targeting BDBV should be generated and tested to help address the growing threat of the virus.”

Stop TB Partnership and Sabin's Boost Community are uniquely primed to connect the immunization and TB communities, to facilitate the generation of actionable evidence, and to build the relationships and shared knowledge needed for an effective preparation and roll-out by countries. post_message: Switching from one vaccine to another is just a matter of out with the old, in with the new, right? Not exactly.   As more than 30 co-authors, including Sabin's Kate Hopkins, PhD, MPH, report in "Accelerating Evidence-Informed Vaccine Introductions: Lessons from the Hexavalent Early Adopters Workshop" in the new issue of the journal Vaccines, there are multiple considerations when bringing a new immunization into a country's immunization schedule, including complex system changes requiring coordinated governance, reliable data systems, domestic financing, and multisectoral collaboration.  The paper presents evidence-based insights on making a successful switch from National Immunization Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs) and Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI) programs of 10 African countries, as well as World Health Organization African Region, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, and consortium partners, who gathered in Senegal last November. It shows the power of Sabin's Regional Peer Learning model/capabilities and helps strengthen policy and operational readiness for countries at different stages of decision-making, planning, and implementation.  See the new article: https://ow.ly/ShmS50Z2nva

post_message: Sabin's Boost Community recently concluded the BoostHER webinar series, a three-part global virtual dialogue spotlighting women’s leadership in immunization and advancing gender-responsive practice across the sector. 🙌  Some key takeaways from these essential conversations:  🔹 Say yes before you feel ready. Women often hold themselves back waiting to feel fully prepared. Stepping into opportunities and learning on the job is how careers accelerate. 🔹 Leadership is a practice, not a position. Regardless of title or role, everyone leads daily through how they show up, communicate, and support others. 🔹 Build a team of mentors, not just one. Different mentors serve different needs. Identify gaps in your skills and goals and find people who speak to each. 🔹 Adaptability is a core leadership skill. The only constant in global health is change. The ability to pivot, learn, and stay flexible determines long-term effectiveness. 🔹 Support other women intentionally. Open doors, make introductions, and lift others up. Collective advancement is a leadership responsibility, not just a personal choice. 🔹 See the full conversation online: https://ow.ly/sbSA50Z9VXv  For even more insights, join the Boost Community — more than 5,000 immunization professionals strong, connecting from around the globe ⤵️ https://ow.ly/xVAl50Z9VXu

post_message: What do a conflict-affected region, an urban slum, and a migrant settlement all have in common?   Turns out, quite a lot.   The new “Social and Behaviour Change to Improve Uptake of Routine Immunization,” a compendium of community-informed and co-designed vaccination interventions from UNICEF, the Sabin Vaccine Institute and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, looks at innovative community-driven social and behavior change strategies to increase vaccine uptake applied in seven very different settings.  Yet there are some common findings:   • Across all seven countries, trust emerged as the most influential factor in caregiver decision-making. • Access continues to be critical. The most impactful strategies combined targeted SBC interventions with efforts to increase service access, such as mobile clinics, improved referral systems and proactive follow-up.   Sabin’s Senior Manager, Vaccine Demand & Implementation, Theresa Sommers, PhD, MPH, is presenting on the findings this week at UNICEF’s 4th International Social and Behavior Change Communication (SBCC) Summit in Panama. Please connect if you are there!   See the full report ⤵️ https://ow.ly/7vhU50ZfelU

post_message: The Sabin Vaccine Institute has been awarded a three-year grant from the Gates Foundation to lead  global communications and advocacy to help protect infants in their first months of life from respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).  RSV is a major cause of severe respiratory illness in infants and the most common viral cause of pneumonia in children. According to the World Health Organization, RSV causes more than 3.6 million hospitalizations and about 100,000 deaths in children under 5 each year.   Approximately half of RSV-related deaths among children occur in infants under six months of age. As maternal RSV immunization moves toward broader global availability, countries have a new opportunity to protect infants during their most vulnerable first months of life.  See more⤵️ https://ow.ly/iUPZ50Zlekb

Spread of diseases like dengue, Oropouche, and yellow fever "all point to the same critical  need: countries require preparedness systems that can detect, verify, and respond to evolving risks before they become larger emergencies." post_message: Preparation is key to success — and representatives from 10 African countries attending the November 2025 Hexavalent Vaccine Early Adopters Workshop in Senegal, co-convened by Sabin and WHO AFRO, learned how to prepare for the switch from pentavalent +IPV to hexavalent vaccines through peers who had already made the transition.  The hexavalent vaccine protects against six diseases in a single shot — improving efficiency and saving lives.   Such Regional Peer Learning models can help strengthen policy and operational readiness for countries at different stages of decision-making, planning, and implementation for vaccine introductions and switches.   See the evidence-based insights surfaced from this workshop in a recently released paper, co-authored by Sabin, WHO Afro, Hexavalent Vaccine (Switch) Assessment Consortium (HeVAC) partners, and workshop participants, in the journal Vaccines ⤵️ https://ow.ly/8sMq50ZnxS6

post_message: Through the Malaria Vaccine Learning Agenda, Sabin and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance brought together four research consortia that represented seven research projects across seven African countries, looking at malaria vaccine uptake. The preliminary findings point to practical solutions: stronger follow-up, better integration with routine child health services, earlier identification of missed children, and greater support for community health workers.   Why this matters: Malaria vaccine uptake falls significantly between the third and fourth doses. Finding solutions that work will ensure greater protection from one of the world’s largest health threats.

post_message: “This work is urgent,” says Sabin Vaccine Institute President of Global Immunization Rebecca Martin on today’s announcement of a new partnership with Population Services International (PSI) aimed at increasing access to vaccines by optimizing the role of pharmacies and other private-sector providers in expanding access to essential health services.  More than 13.5 million children worldwide received no vaccine protection in their first year of life in 2025, according to the latest WHO/UNICEF Estimates of Vaccination Coverage released in July 2026.   The collaboration brings together Sabin’s expertise in immunization and generating and translating evidence for vaccine policy and program implementation with PSI’s experience implementing, scaling and strengthening health delivery in communities to  connect people where they are with high-quality services through providers they know and trust.  See the press release ⤵️ https://ow.ly/LLv450ZNpNR

Sabin and STOP TB Partnership host "Preparing for Future TB Vaccine Introduction: Brazil, Indonesia, and South Africa."  📅 Thursday, October 8 ⏰ 1:00–2:30 p.m. UTC 🌐 Simultaneous French interpretation will be available  New #tuberculosis vaccines are approaching a critical stage of development, making it essential for countries to begin preparing for their introduction now. Partnership between national TB and Immunization programs and partners are particularly strategic to make this work.  Together, speakers will discuss:  🔹 Current country readiness for the introduction of new TB vaccines 🔹 The roles of TB and immunization programs in planning and implementation 🔹 Opportunities to strengthen coordination across programs 🔹 Key policy, delivery, communication, and community engagement considerations 🔹 Practical lessons that can inform early readiness efforts in other countries 🔹 Country presentations will be followed by a moderated panel discussion and an opportunity for participants to submit questions to the speakers.
